levels.title: ALOHA Party
levels.story: In Crowded Plaza, villagers shout their announcements all at once. If two shout together, nobody understands either. Mayor Moss asks Kit to find a fair way to share the plaza without anyone in charge.

everyday.scene: In a group voice chat, two friends start talking at exactly the same moment. Both stop, both start again, and it happens twice more before someone says "you go first".
everyday.question: When nobody is in charge, how can a crowd share one channel without constantly talking over each other?
everyday.answer: With simple rules. In ALOHA, you just send, and if your frame collides, you wait a random time and try again. A cleverer version, slotted ALOHA, agrees on beats so that stations can only start at the start of a slot, which halves the chance of an overlap.

lessons.title: One plaza, many voices
text: Some networks are shared: all stations use the same channel, like a plaza where everyone's voice carries. If two frames overlap, that's a collision, and both are lost.
A part of the data link layer, the MAC sub-layer, decides who may send next.

Fixed turns (static allocation) are simple, but waste time when stations are quiet. Letting stations send when they have something to say (dynamic allocation) is more efficient, but needs rules to handle collisions.

terms.meaning: One channel that many stations send on.
Two frames overlap, so both are lost.
Medium access control: the rules for who sends when on a shared channel.

Idea

lessons.title: Pure ALOHA: just talk
text: In pure ALOHA a station sends whenever it likes. If no ACK comes back, it waits a random time and sends again. Waiting a random time matters: two stations that collided won't both retry at the same instant.
A frame is in danger if another one starts within one frame time before it or one frame time after. That danger window is the vulnerable period: two frame times.
Example: a frame takes 10 ms to send. Anyone who starts within 10 ms before or 10 ms after wrecks it: a 20 ms window.

terms.meaning: How long it takes to send one frame.
The window of time in which another frame would collide with yours.
Each station picks its own delay, so they don't clash again.

predict.prompt: A frame takes 4 ms to send. How long is its vulnerable period in pure ALOHA?
predict.answer: 8 ms: 4 ms before plus 4 ms after.

deeper.title: The formula
text: If G is the average number of frames offered per frame time, pure ALOHA's throughput is S = G × e^(−2G), where e is about 2.718. It peaks at G = 0.5, where S is about 18.4%.

lessons.title: Slotted ALOHA: talk on the beat
text: Slotted ALOHA cuts time into slots, each exactly one frame long. A station may only start at the beginning of a slot. Frames now either overlap completely or not at all.
The vulnerable period halves to one frame time, and the best throughput roughly doubles. Throughput is the share of time the channel carries good frames.
Look at the table. Both methods get worse if too much traffic is offered, because more frames mean more collisions.

terms.meaning: A fixed window of time, one frame long, when a station may start sending.
Frames the stations try to send, per frame time.
The share of time that carries good frames (not collisions).

lessons.diagramCaption: Throughput for both methods. Each peaks and then falls.

deeper.title: The formula
text: Slotted ALOHA's throughput is S = G × e^(−G), which peaks at G = 1 with S = 1 ÷ e, about 36.8%.

fieldNotes.title: A radio network across the islands
fieldNotes.text: ALOHA grew out of ALOHAnet, a radio network that began running in 1971 to connect computers on different Hawaiian islands. Its idea, "just send, and retry after a random wait if it fails", led to Ethernet.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check the year (1971) and the claim that ALOHA inspired Ethernet.

summary: You saw why overlapping frames are lost, why pure ALOHA has a two-frame danger window, and how slotted ALOHA halves it by agreeing on a beat.
Mayor Moss claps. "Much better than shouting," he says. "But can't we simply listen first?"

mistake.title: Expecting more traffic to mean more throughput
mistake.text: More offered load helps only up to a point. Past the peak, extra frames cause extra collisions and the channel carries less. The best load for slotted ALOHA is G = 1, and for pure ALOHA it's G = 0.5.

levels.title: Listen Before You Talk
levels.story: Mayor Moss has a better idea for the plaza: listen first, and speak only if nobody else is talking. Kit has to find out whether that is enough.

everyday.scene: At a dinner table you wait for a gap before you speak. Now and then two people start at the same instant, both stop, laugh, and try again.
everyday.question: Is listening first enough to stop all collisions?
everyday.answer: No. Two stations can start at the very same moment, and signals take time to travel, so a station may not yet hear that someone else has started. So stations also listen while they send, and stop as soon as they notice a collision. This is called CSMA/CD.

lessons.title: Listen first: CSMA
text: CSMA stands for carrier sense multiple access, which just means listen before you send. If the channel is idle, send. If it's busy, there are three choices.

1-persistent: keep listening, and send the moment it's free. Non-persistent: wait a random time, then listen again. p-persistent: when it's free, send with probability p, otherwise wait a slot and check again.
Each has a trade-off, shown in the table.

terms.meaning: Listening to find out whether someone else is sending.
Keeps listening while the channel is busy.

lessons.title: Collisions still happen: CSMA/CD
text: Signals take time to travel, so two far-apart stations may both think the channel is idle. CSMA/CD adds collision detection: while sending, the station keeps listening. If it hears a garbled mix, it stops and sends a short jam signal.
How long must a frame be? The sender must still be sending when the news of a collision returns. In the worst case that's a round trip: twice the one-way delay.
Example: a 1,000,000 bits per second cable with a 0.2 ms one-way delay has a 0.4 ms round trip. 1,000,000 × 0.0004 = 400 bits, so frames must be at least 400 bits long.

terms.meaning: Carrier sense multiple access with collision detection.
A short burst that tells everyone a collision happened.
The time for a signal to go to the far end and for news to come back.

predict.prompt: The one-way delay on a cable is 0.5 ms. How long must a sender keep sending so it can still hear a collision from the far end?
predict.answer: At least a round trip: 1 ms.

deeper.title: Why Ethernet frames have a minimum size
text: Classic Ethernet sets a minimum frame of 64 bytes for exactly this reason. If the cable were longer or the bit rate higher, the minimum frame would need to be longer too.

references.title: Wikipedia: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection
Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, section 2.6 Multi-access networks (Ethernet)

lessons.title: Waiting a random time
text: After a collision, every station involved waits a random time before trying again. If they all picked from the same tiny range they might clash again, so the range grows.
That's binary exponential backoff. After the 1st collision pick a random wait from 0 or 1 slots. After the 2nd, from 0 to 3. After the 3rd, from 0 to 7. The range doubles each time.
Busy networks spread out quickly, and quiet ones don't wait long.

fieldNotes.title: Why Wi-Fi can't listen while it talks
fieldNotes.text: On a cable, a station can listen while it sends. A radio can't: its own signal is far too strong for it to hear anyone else. So Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) instead of collision detection: it tries hard not to collide in the first place.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check that this is a fair simple description of why Wi-Fi uses avoidance rather than detection.

summary: You listened before sending, saw why collisions still happen, worked out the minimum frame length, and used random backoff to recover.
Moss tips his hat. "The plaza has never been so polite," he says.

mistake.title: Thinking listening first prevents every collision
mistake.text: Listening reduces collisions but can't stop them all, because of the delay between a station starting to send and the others hearing it. That is why CSMA/CD also listens while sending and backs off afterwards.

levels.title: Hidden Hills
levels.story: Beyond the plaza, hills block the signals between the farms. Kit's wireless lantern can't see everyone, so listening first no longer works. Kit needs a way for stations to ask each other for permission.

everyday.scene: Two friends stand on opposite sides of a hill, and both text you at the same moment. They can't see or hear each other, but you're in the middle and get both messages at once, jumbled.
everyday.question: How can two wireless stations collide when each checked that the channel was quiet?
everyday.answer: Because they can't hear each other. This is the hidden terminal problem. The fix is to ask first: the sender sends a short request, and the receiver's reply is heard by everyone nearby, even stations the sender can't hear.

lessons.title: Hidden terminals
text: Picture three stations in a row: A, B and C. A and C can both hear B, but a hill blocks them from hearing each other.
A listens: quiet. C listens: quiet. Both send to B at the same time. B hears a jumble. A and C are hidden from each other, even though they both reach B.
Listening before sending is useless here, because the sender can't hear the station that will cause the collision.

terms.meaning: A device that sends or receives, like a phone or laptop.
How far a station's signal reaches.
A station that can't hear another sender but can still collide with it at the receiver.

lessons.diagramCaption: A and C are hidden from each other.

predict.prompt: A is sending to B. C listens first. Does C hear A?
predict.answer: No. The hill blocks the signal, so C thinks the channel is quiet.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, section 2.7 Wireless

lessons.title: Exposed terminals
text: The opposite problem: B is sending to A. C hears B's signal, so it stays quiet. But C wanted to send to D, who is far from B and A. That transmission wouldn't have bothered anyone.
C is an exposed terminal: it waits for no good reason. Nothing is damaged, but capacity is wasted.
The two problems are mirror images: hidden terminals cause collisions, and exposed terminals cause needless waiting.

terms.meaning: A station that stays quiet because it hears another sender, even though its own frame wouldn't hurt the receiver.

head: Problem
What goes wrong
Result
rows: Can't hear the sender who will collide at the receiver
Hears a sender that wouldn't interfere

predict.prompt: B is sending to A. C hears B but wants to send to D, who is out of B's range. Is C hidden or exposed?

lessons.title: Ask first: RTS and CTS
text: Before sending a long frame, the sender sends a very short RTS: request to send. The receiver replies with a CTS: clear to send.
The CTS is heard by every station near the receiver, including ones the sender can't hear. Any station that hears the CTS stays quiet for the whole transfer.
In the hill example, C hears B's CTS and waits. If two RTS messages collide, little is lost, because they're short.

terms.meaning: Request to send: a short "may I send?" frame.
Clear to send: the receiver's reply, heard by all its neighbours.

predict.prompt: Why is it useful that the receiver, not the sender, sends the CTS?
predict.answer: The receiver is the one in the middle, so its signal reaches the stations that would collide at it, including ones the sender can't hear.

deeper.title: The cost of asking
text: The RTS/CTS handshake takes time. For tiny frames it can cost more than a collision would, which is why Wi-Fi makes RTS/CTS optional and usually only uses it for large frames. The idea comes from a protocol called MACA.

references.title: Wikipedia: MACA (Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance for Wireless)

fieldNotes.title: RTS/CTS in your Wi-Fi
fieldNotes.text: Wi-Fi routers support RTS/CTS, but it's usually only switched on for big frames, because the handshake costs time. On a crowded network with a lot of hidden stations, turning it on can help.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check the wording about when RTS/CTS is used in Wi-Fi.

summary: You found out why listening first fails behind a hill, how hidden and exposed terminals differ, and how RTS and CTS make everyone nearby wait.
Kit climbs to the top of Hidden Hills and looks back. The plaza is calm at last. But the road from here leads out of the valley, towards the Router Ranch. The letter has a long way to go.

mistake.title: Thinking carrier sensing is enough on wireless
mistake.text: Listening works only if you can hear every station that might collide with you. On wireless, hills and distance hide stations from each other, so stations ask first with RTS and CTS.
